summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) at 13.0% of firms in the latest reading, up from 7.9% in the prior period. The question asked was whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the survey first asked it in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it describes the sector as a whole rather than any single mode.

The most visible deployment is autonomous driving. Aurora describes self-driving freight powered by the Aurora Driver, built with hardware and software it says is backed by verifiable AI, and quotes a Werner executive on a pilot hauling freight between Fort Worth and El Paso under a hybrid model of professional drivers and the Aurora Driver. Waymo, which began as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served its first fully autonomous rides in 2015, publishes a safety program and supports the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy by advancing safer vehicles and safer speeds through its autonomous ride-hailing service. The American Trucking Associations appears here as the trade body for the industry, with more than 37,000 members, rather than as a source of adoption numbers.

AI is also deployed in the less visible layers of the sector. Samsara says its connected operations platform serves 20,000+ operations and reports 380,000+ accidents prevented, driven by AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, and automated coaching, alongside predictive analytics and equipment management. C.H. Robinson describes autonomous logistics orchestration in which a supply chain analyzes, decides, executes, and improves across every shipment, and runs an AI assistant on its own site. Wärtsilä cites AI-driven predictive analytics among the tools it offers marine customers for decarbonisation. Airbus frames its innovation work around a decarbonised, connected and autonomous future for aerospace.

Money and vendor activity concentrate around the large platforms and equipment makers rather than around small operators. The material names Aurora, Waymo, Samsara, C.H. Robinson, Wärtsilä, Airbus, and, in this site's own tracking, Palantir as an enterprise AI platform used by airlines and rail operators for fleet and crew optimization, and Mobileye as the supplier of computer-vision stacks in driver-assist systems. This site also maintains a Robotics Models catalogue drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, listing the 1000 most-downloaded open robotics models with licence, downloads, and release date, refreshed daily. No source in the material reports a dollar figure or a return-on-investment calculation for any deployment.

The regulatory posture is set by safety agencies and international bodies. EASA's Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 sets out the agency's vision for safety and ethical considerations of AI in aviation, with a comprehensive action plan, conceptual guidance deliverables, and anticipated rulemaking, and is described as a living document amended once a year. The IMO adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, effective 1 July 2026, providing voluntary, goal-based guidance for the safe design, operation, and certification of such ships, complementing existing maritime regulations and designed to facilitate a future transition into a mandatory instrument. The IMO states that at present there are no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or remotely controlled, though trials have shown larger remotely controlled and autonomous ships are feasible. The material also notes that the FAA's innovation work and EASA's roadmap are the regulatory record for AI flight systems, automated risk management, and eVTOL certification.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources point to a sector where measured adoption is still modest but where the leading deployments sit in safety-critical and network-scale functions: driving, fleet monitoring, freight matching, and vessel and aircraft operations. The evidence offered is operational and safety-oriented, such as Waymo's published safety record and Samsara's accident-prevention figure, not financial. The gating factors named in the material are regulators and classification bodies, EASA and the IMO in particular, and the IMO's caution that autonomous systems introduce different operational risks requiring alternative approaches. Where the sources are silent, on cost, on payback, and on adoption broken out by mode, this analysis does not fill the gap.

https://www.samsara.com/.brief: Samsara claims its connected operations platform supports more than 20,000 operations in improving safety, cutting costs, and running smarter. The platform analyzes data to provide AI-driven alerts, predictive analytics, and actionable insights that help spot risks and optimize operations. According to Samsara, its AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching, and other safety technologies have prevented over 380,000 accidents. The system includes cameras and video AI, multicam support, driver experience tools, driver coaching, drowsiness detection, safety reporting & insights, and equipment management.

https://www.trucking.org/.brief: ATA, the American Trucking Association, says it is the largest and most comprehensive national trade association for trucking. It reports that Miguel Corral, a UPS driver, was named Bendix Grand Champion at the 2026 National Truck Driving & Step Van Championships. ATA says it has more than 37,000 members, including carriers, suppliers, shippers, and professionals, and that it works to influence government policy, educate stakeholders, and host events that bring together all parts of the industry.

https://www.wartsila.com/.brief: Wärtsilä describes itself as a global leader in technologies and lifecycle solutions for the marine and energy markets. The company states that while no single solution will carry the transition, most of the technology needed to decarbonise already exists. It cites engines that run flexibly on low- and zero-carbon fuels and AI-driven predictive analytics among the tools it offers customers for their decarbonisation efforts. Wärtsilä also reports it will supply a 282 MW onsite power solution for a U.S. data center, which it links to AI growth intensifying demand for reliable power.

https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/re.brief: The EASA has published an Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 that outlines the Agency's approach to safety and ethical considerations for AI in aviation. The roadmap provides an action plan for the EASA AI Programme, including conceptual guidance and anticipated rulemaking activities, and serves as a basis for stakeholder discussions. As a living document, it will be updated annually and refined through stakeholder exchanges and the Agency's ongoing practical work on AI development.

https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTo.brief: The IMO introduced a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS Code) in May 2026, which became effective on 1 July 2026. A ship is considered a MASS only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support crew functions and it holds a valid MASS Safety Certificate; enhanced automation alone does not qualify. The Code offers voluntary, technology-neutral guidance that complements existing regulations and defines operating conditions, limits, and responses when those limits are exceeded, creating a “goal-based framework” for safe design, operation, and certification. Trials under interim MSC 110 guidelines in June 2019 have shown that larger remotely controlled and autonomous ships are feasible, and while no SOLAS cargo ships are yet operating autonomously, the IMO anticipates commercial service in the near future with a gradual evolution toward more advanced MASS. An IMO seminar in April 2024 addressed the implications, challenges, and opportunities of MASS for ports and public authorities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open robotics models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and is refreshed daily. The site states the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. It also describes a search function covering the full text of its published pages, which it says are all built from one database spanning topics such as state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies and a research library. The page was last verified on 2026-10-05 and offers a citation format for the catalogue.
